html:
Things Fall Apart is the first novel of the Nigerian writer Chinua Achebe, published in London in 1958. It follows Okonkwo, a proud wrestler and leader of Umuofia, a fictional group of Igbo villages, in the late 1800s, and shows how his world breaks apart when British missionaries and officials arrive.

The book has three parts:

  • Igbo life before the colonisers: yam farming, councils of elders, festivals, religion, marriage and many proverbs.
  • Okonkwo's seven years of exile after he kills a man by accident.
  • His return, as Christian converts and a colonial court change the village. It ends with his death and a British officer planning a book on "pacifying" the tribes of the Lower Niger, in which Okonkwo will get a paragraph.

Achebe wrote partly against European novels, such as Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness, that showed Africans as people without history or culture. He wrote in English, while working at the Nigerian Broadcasting Corporation, and took the title from a line in W. B. Yeats's poem "The Second Coming".

The novel came out two years before Nigeria's independence and became the most widely read work of modern African literature, translated into dozens of languages. It led the African Writers Series, which Achebe edited from 1962. He followed it with No Longer at Ease and Arrow of God, together called the African trilogy.
